text_fidelity_a:
SYMA Mini Drones for Kids or Adults, Easy Indoor Flying Helicopter with Auto Hovering,3D Flip,Headless Pocket Quadcopters UFO Toy Gift for Boys Girls Disclaimer: I own a DJI Mavic Pro, and started out with a Holy Stone quadcopter. I've flown smaller ones like the DJI Spark and the DJI Tello, which is similar in size. I would say that for the price, this is a five-star drone. You get a lot for 35 dollars. Compared to other drones, I would say that there are certain improvements that could be made but those drones are much, much more expensive.
Pros:
Small manageable size - the drone is quite small, which is nice because it lends itself to indoor flight and easy travel. It is about 4.5 inches by 4.5 inches for a length and width, and the diagonal rotor distance is about 5 inches, while to entire copter stands at about 1.25 inches. This, as I said, is nice for indoor flight and you don't have to worry too much about hitting someone. You can also easily launch it and land it from and on your hand.

Robust and reasonably crash proof - The blade guards proved themselves quite useful, as I bumped it into walls several times, and the guards did their job. The copter simply bounced off the wall and continued flying. Additionally, when I was testing it, the drone died while flying. I knew this was coming, as I could feel the responsiveness beginning to slow and the flip function would no longer work. The drone fell from about 12 feet in the air onto the blacktop. I didn't notice and dings, dents, or scar=tches, and once it was charged, it flew fine.

Quiet - The drone has a shrill high pitched sound as it flies. It isn't too loud, and I could talk to those next to me while flying without having to raise my voice while the copter was only a few feet away.

Auto-flip function - This is fun. Executed, the drone flips in your specified direction, rolling quickly left, right, forward of backward and returning to hovering once completed. The flip function does not work once the battery drops below a certain percentage.

LED lights for battery and connectivity - These are easy to see when on the ground and display info about the battery when charging or low, and connectivity when first powered on. The rear lights are green, and the ones in the front are red, but they can be hard to see in daylight once it gets more than about 30 feet away.

Good range. I flew the drone about 70 or 80 feet away laterally without any problems, and about 40 feet up before coming down for fear of wind gusts. It worked fine, with no noticeable latency.

Headless Mode - Great function for learning pilots, especially for a drone like this that has no camera feed. However, the instructions are quite confusing on how to engage this and it took me a solid 5 minutes of fiddling with the controls to get it to work. To get this to work, take off, hold the button a the top left of the controller until it starts beeping, and then push the stick forward. The forward-facing direction will remain that relative forward until this function is disengaged.

Cons:
Disproportionate flight to charge time ratio - According to the user manual, this charge time is about 70 minutes, while the flight time is around 5 minutes while hovering. I, however, found that it took about 35 minutes (charging for a wall outlet) for a full charge from dropping out of the sky dead. The flight time that I got was about 6 minutes, doing maneuvers, flips, climbing, falling, accelerating and decelerating. Still, I think this could be improved, and, as there are no removable batteries you can plug in once another is dead, I make using the drone for more than 10 minutes hard.
Poor wind resistance - This thing blows outside with the slightest breeze. Inside, the flight trim is hard to adjust, and outside, it is not worth it. I found myself constantly adjusting to compensate for any wind.
Instructions aren't very clear - I found myself struggling to engage Headless mode, as well as find things within the manual. There are occasional typos, and the layout is confusing.
Joysticks don't articulate much - This is actually somewhat annoying. there isn't much height to the sticks, and they don't move around much, making any more precise movements difficult. Additionally, the other buttons on the controller are somewhat difficult to press.

I liked this drone, especially for the price. This would be great for any kid, or even as a starting copter for someone who wants to see if they are interested in them. I like the size, durability, and flip function, but the battery life and wind resistance are something to consider.
text_fidelity_b: SYMA Mini Drones for Kids or Adults, Easy Indoor Flying Helicopter with Auto Hovering,3D Flip,Headless Pocket Quadcopters UFO Toy Gift for Boys Girls

Thames & Kosmos TK1 Telescope Plus Astronomy Educational Science Kit | Refractor 60/700 | Aluminum Full Size Tripod with Altazimuth Mount | 35X, 70X, 140X Power | Parents' Choice Recommended The telescope itself is really very good. Even with the lowest magnification lens attached The Housemate and I were able to see Saturn and discern the gap between the planet and its rings. With a higher magnification, things became much clearer, and even more exciting. The first clear image of the moon took my breath away.

The drawbacks? It's very hard to use standing up. I realize it's made for children, but I think a taller tripod might have been a plus here. Even sitting we had to hunch down to see anything at a 45 degree angle or above. Also, the viewfinder did not help at all. I found all the objects we wanted to see by sighting along the barrel of the telescope itself. Now possibly I attached the viewfinder the wrong way, though there really only seems to be one way to do it. Either way, we saw what we intended to see which made the exercise worthwhile.

Why a telescope? Aren't you and your children worth it? Don't you want to learn more about even our part of the universe? This is an amazing gift for the children in your life, or even for yourself. It's lightweight and easy to transport and with the help of something like Google Sky, you can figure out what it is you're looking at with ease. It's a step on the road to becoming better educated in Astronomy, and it should spark a sense of wonder anyone who looks up and longs to know more.

Insect Lore - Butterfly Growing Kit - Butterfly Habitat Kit with Voucher to Redeem 5 Caterpillars, STEM Journal, Butterfly Feeder & More – Life Science & STEM Education – Butterfly Science Kit The Live Butterfly Garden by Insect Lore is a fun, hands- on educational experience that is certain to appeal to even the most stubborn, disinterested child. With the Live Butterfly Garden, children get to observe the process of metamorphosis, right before their eyes. Starting with caterpillars, children watch the little critters eat food, create a cocoon, and then transform into fully grown adult butterflies. The butterflies can then be observed in their habitat for a while before setting free.

This butterfly garden is great for dozens of reasons, the most obvious of which is the educational value. Reading about insects and metamorphosis is one thing, but seeing the process live is another thing entirely. Kids get to learn how caterpillars/butterflies live, eat, and thrive; how to care for them; etc. They get to observe the caterpillars and butterflies at play and watch the butterflies eat their food, which is provided in the package. The caterpillars that come with the Live Butterfly Garden are painted ladies, which are not very common and will not be recognized by most children. However, most kids won't care- the fun of watching these small caterpillars transform into butterflies will have many kids gazing in awe, and prompt them to ask many questions.

This educational toy is a huge hit and my kids loved it, but there were a few small issues. One was waiting for the caterpillars to arrive in the mail. To get the caterpillars, you have to mail in an included certificate, along with a check, and then wait. It seems like an eternity, especially from the perspective of young children, and it took longer than expected. Anther problem was parting with the butterflies. Once you have the caterpillars and they have transformed into adult butterflies, the next problem will be setting them free. Kids will grow attached to their small, winged friends and will not want to let them go. Another minor issue is with the transferring of the caterpillars from their small container- the one you receive in the mail- into the actual habitat. The container that the caterpillars arrive in has a paper area at the top, where the caterpillars will hang as they spin their cocoons. This paper section is fairly easy to remove, but the problem is that the cocoons are very delicately attached, and that means that some will fall off when the transfer is made. You will need to pin this piece of paper to the inside of the butterfly garden, but the kit doesn't include any pins. Safety pins or straight pins work, and it would have been nice if these were included in the kit.

Still, when all factors are considered, the Live Butterfly Garden is worth the purchase and young children will enjoy the educational experience. Sure, it could be improved a little bit by making a few minor changes, but this is still a very good toy and considering my kid's fascination with the process, along with the educational value, it earns an easy recommendation.
text_fidelity_b: Insect Lore - Butterfly Growing Kit - Butterfly Habitat Kit with Voucher to Redeem 5 Caterpillars, STEM Journal, Butterfly Feeder & More – Life Science & STEM Education – Butterfly Science Kit

fansmart 39" Pull -Along Wagon for Kids with Pulling Wood Railing Panels Outdoor Wagon 10" All Terrain Air Tires 330 lbs Capacity for Beach, Garden, Sporting Events, Park（Red） I got this 'Lil Red Wagon' from Fansmart mainly for around the house use. I have a much MUCH larger garden wagon that can be pulled by hand or hooked up to your lawn and garden mower/tractor. But, it's just not convenient for doing simple things around the flower garden. This Fansmart wagon is great for that. Putting it together, I noted a few things. 1) Don't overtighten the acorn nuts. You will pop the caps right off. 2) The wood stake and slate side panels are NOT the most solidly built. The wood is soft pine and the panels are just stapled together. My advice would be to coat them very well with some clear polyurethane or other wood preservative before assembly. And, don't be too rough or careless when working with them. it's okay to put a load against them. Jut understand that there are limitations on how much abuse they can take. 3) When putting the cotter pins through the axles, to hold the wheels on, make sure you bend them all the way around the axles, to prevent any chance of a puncture or laceration from the sharp ends of the cotter pins. 4) Use your common sense in assembling the front yoke / truck assembly. The illustration is not that detailed. But, it's fairly simple. The finished front end will NOT be that tightly fitted when you're done. That's okay. It's the way it was designed. 5) The rounded pan head of all the bolts going through the pan of the wagon go ON THE INSIDE of the pan, not the outside. Even then, the heads do not seat perfectly into the holes. They do have an edge that can snag on bagged materials like mulch, potting soil, etc. My advice would be to lay a piece of cardboard or something in the bed of the wagon. The would both prevent tears in your bagged materials AND protect the finish of the wagon.

I've been using mine for hauling heavy plants around and even moving frozen goods from the deep freeze to the snow bank, during this 'winter storm of the century' that we had down here in Texas. The power was out for four days and I didn't want to lose roughly $700 in venison. Lil Red did the trick.

If anyone is old enough to remember the 'Radio Flyer' wagons that were sold a few decades ago, this wagon is kind of like that. But, not as big and not as heavily constructed. However, this wagon is good enough quality, for the price, to still earn a five star rating from me.
text_fidelity_b: fansmart 39" Pull -Along Wagon for Kids with Pulling Wood Railing Panels Outdoor Wagon 10" All Terrain Air Tires 330 lbs Capacity for Beach, Garden, Sporting Events, Park（Red）

Prime Climb Great game for helping kids understand factors and learn their multiplication/division (and addition/subtraction) facts, plus it's FUN! The part that initially drew me in for where my kids are was the color coding of the basic primes, and by extension the use of those colors to represent factors in the products. Then, it arrived and the gameplay was really fun--there are two ten sided dice and you can add, subtract, multiply or divide the number you are on by each die in turn to move. If you land on a prime you get to draw a Prime Card, which you can either use right away or save for later to benefit yourself or target an opponent, depending on whether the card is an Action card or Keeper. The first person to move both pawns to 101 wins. If you get tired of the standard rules, though, they apparently have some variations here: [...] but I have not yet tried any--looking forward to doing so after we've played through a few more times.

Oh and keep in mind that it takes longer the more players there are--folks with younger kids might want to keep it to 2 or 3 players so it doesn't go so long, or modify the rules so people don't get sent back to start so often. I'm sure there are cooperative ways to play too if that's more up someone's alley, like it was for us when the kids were younger.

SYMA X22W Mini Drone with Camera Live Video FPV Pocket Drone for Kids and Beginners, RC Quadcopter with App Control, Altitude Hold, 3D Flips, Headless Mode and Bonus Battery, Red I always wanted to have a small drone to be able to inspect parts of my house inaccessible to me like my roof and the gutters. I was surprised how small the drone was when I received it. It fit in the palm of my hand. After reading through the directions twice, I thought I had a basic idea on how to operate the drone. I downloaded the app, connected to it via WiFi and had the propellers spinning up and that’s when things kinda lost control. The drone flew up a few feet but also flew forward (or backwards) even though I wasn’t touching the right control stick which is supposed to do that. Up and down seemed to be working fine, but with the drone constantly flying sideways, it was impossible to control properly. Even when using the right control stick, it seemed to only acknowledge forwards, and wouldn’t respond to the other direction. Then the drone suddenly dropped the WiFi connection within 10 minutes. Powering off and on didn’t fix it. I took the battery out, put it back in and was connected again for a minute or two before the battery just died completely. Yes, I fully charged the battery before use. Surely this products battery should last more than 15 minutes of intermittent usage.
Overall, as someone familiar with remote control devices and technology, I found this drone difficult to control and hence no fun to use.
text_fidelity_b: SYMA X22W Mini Drone with Camera Live Video FPV Pocket Drone for Kids and Beginners, RC Quadcopter with App Control, Altitude Hold, 3D Flips, Headless Mode and Bonus Battery, Red

Girl Scouts Cookie Oven Reminiscent of the iconic Easy Bake oven, this toy is a fun way for kids to learn about baking. small but sturdy, it has a thick and durable plastic housing. The green color is similar to a girl scout's uniform. It is accented with purple and pink. Baking is actually easy. One starts by preheating the oven by turning the pink plastic dial on the front. It takes roughly five minutes for the oven to preheat. the LED light in the oven comes on when it is ready and is designed to help gauge the progress of the cookies. Unfortunately it fails to illuminate much of the oven. a brighter light cold help you see more than maybe the closest two cookies.

Making the cookies is simple. The included pan feels like heavy aluminum foil. give it a generous shot of cooking spray before use. It is not dishwasher safe and you will probably want to hand wash it between batches. There is a syringe with which to measure the water that is required for the mix. The syringe is actually kind of cool. The markings are easy to read. Caution your child to resist the temptation to shoot it out into the bowl (or at you) as it will make a mess. Stir and drop on the cookie sheet. Insert the sheet into the oven and set your timer. a timer/clock is not included in the device which is a pity. It takes about ten minutes for them to bake. They are then slid into the cooling chamber where they sit for another ten minutes. the cookies are then ready to come out of the oven. There is a pink spatula like tool which can help pull the tray out or you can just use a potholder or oven mitt. The cookies are then placed on a plate lined with waxed paper. the thin mint mix which came with the oven also has a pouch of chocolate chips for the frosting. The chips are melted on warming station on the top of the oven. the outside and the warming station do not get hot which is great for safety. But that is not great for melting things. After ten minutes, the chips still were not melted to so I popped them in the microwave. The frosting spread easily and the cookies tasted good. the cookies are small and, frankly, the Girl Scout cookie monopoly has nothing to fear.

This is a fun toy for a child, boy or girl, interested in baking. It is easy to use and the outside does not get too hot. the measuring is fun with the syringe and the child is rewarded with a tasty treat for following the directions. there are a wide variety of replacement mixes available including oatmeal, peanut butter, trefoils, sugar, chocolate chip, coconut caramel and PB sandwich. they range in price from around 46.99 for a single pack to 14.99 for a three pack and are available on amazon as well as retailers like Walmart and Toys R Us.

The downside is that it does take time so be sure to have other activities for the kids during the baking and cooling processes. I wish the oven light was brighter and that it had a built in timer/clock. It takes quite a bit of time for six little cookies. while the color scheme makes sense since it is marketed under the Girl Scout label, it may be off putting to boys. Younger ones probably won't care but the older ones may object to the vivid pink spatula and feminine styling. The cookies are not an exact replica but an approximate. tasty but definitely not the real deal. I would have liked to see some "from scratch" recipes included. Children will learn some basic concepts about baking here including timing, preheating, measuring and mixing. But they won't learn about temperatures, ingredients and nutrition. But this is a toy that may encourage a baby baker to hone the craft as he gets older and develop an understanding and appreciation for the art.
text_fidelity_b: Girl Scouts Cookie Oven

text_fidelity_a:
IDO3D Pen and Ink Up to 25 Projects Print System - 5 pens What a great creative art toy. You can do literally anything with this and takes your sketches off the paper and into three dimensions. I am amazed at the ways the kids put this into practice, and it kept them engrossed for hours with only a couple squabbles over people hogging this color or that. I'll get more into what we did below. But first, What you get and How this works.

This product is a hardening gel that can be squeezed into shapes using plastic forms. There are several forms that come with the kit, a flat sheet of plastic and a couple rounded forms for creating spherical shapes. The flat clear piece is great for tracing images so even young kids can achieve the shapes they desire. Also, we used it to make other curves to help flesh out animal shapes, but that proved a little more difficult.

Once you have drawn your shapes with one of the gel pens, you can use the UV flashlight to harden the pieces to make them retain the shapes you want. Then you can peel them off the plastic forms or sheet and cement elements together into three dimensional structures. The possibilities are endless and only limited by creativity. Our kids started out by tracing the provided dinosaurs and moved on to tracing other dinos from various books until they had a small forest of dinos and trees.

Warnings and caveats: I'm a little leery of the chemically nature of this toy. There are warnings to avoid skin contact in light. This put me a little on edge and I wanted to supervise our 8 through 14 year olds to make sure it was not getting on skin or other stuff. Also, this does take a bit of artistic ability. It can be as free form as you want it to be, but we did have some frustration when younger kids could not recreate the stuff the older kids were building. But for the most part it was very conducive to creativity.

Also, the end products are a little sticky. So they don't seem like you can play with your creations, but you can make wonderful visual art. We have a nice little dino diorama on our book shelf now and the kids seem pretty proud of it. The inks are also a little messy, so make sure your in a cleanable area.

Personally, I think this is one of the most wonderfully novel and creative ideas I've seen in a while. I will be picking up some for the kids on my Christmas list, and look forward to refilling our supply.
text_fidelity_b: IDO3D Pen and Ink Up to 25 Projects Print System - 5 pens

text_fidelity_a:
Asmodee Hit Z Road This is a very silly game, despite the theme. Not a gory or cartoonish zombie game, it really could be almost anything in place of them: Mad Max-style marauders, for instance. What's nice about that is, if you're anything like me, and you're totally over all types of zombie games, you will still be able to play Hit Z Road.

This game is really a push your luck dice rolling game with auctions. You're trying to survive until the end of the road, and you need to make some meaningful choices along the way that could make your journey much easier, or much more daring. There is some player elimination, but it's not one of those "you can die on the first turn" types of eliminations - our earliest death was about 10 minutes before the end of the game.

I think a lot of people will find the artwork on this game to be fantastic, and I have to admit that it is daring, different, and one of the most unique looking games out there. While I can admire the work that went into it, the art just doesn't appeal to me.

The name, by the way, might be one of the worst in the history of board gaming.
text_fidelity_b: Asmodee Hit Z Road

text_fidelity_a:
Boardwalk Arcade Pop-A-Shot This is video pinball as it used to be, before today's highly sophisticated physics simulators: floaty ball mechanics, dumbed down special features, bizarre flipper behavior, etc. Which is what I expected.

But I have to say, I'm impressed at the care they put into it nevertheless. They carefully reproduced the major playfield features and loops, the special modes, the multiballs, the spinning pizza. They made the marquee its whole own separate screen so they could have the interactive elements. They have a clever alternative for the plunger (hold down the button for longer to shoot harder). The flipper buttons on the side can get a little finger-cramping, so they put duplicates on the back of the unit so you can hold the whole unit. And, for better or for worse, they reproduced all of the boys' voices. Ugh. And unless I'm mistaken, unlike most of the Tiny Arcade series, it actually saves your high scores.

It's not all good - the "Start Game"/"Game Over" text is hilariously blocky, like an Atari 2600 game, and it pops up on the playfield. I don't know why they didn't put it on the marquee LCD where it belonged. The ball vibrates weirdly on the habitrails. A couple times, particularly in multiball, I've had the ball just simply fall through the hinge of the flipper. But these aren't huge concerns, and they're easily laughed off.

One warning for sensitive and/or young users: I've always thought the original pinball game's marquee's presentation of April was excessively sexy (she's a hero in her own right, not eye candy, darn it) but in the cut down version it looks like... uh, something else entirely.

All in all, this way exceeded my expectations. And it's actually quite fun! I'm not interested in the other "boardwalk arcade" games so far, but I'd gladly buy more pinball games like this one if they're at a similar level of playability.
text_fidelity_b: Boardwalk Arcade Pop-A-Shot

text_fidelity_a:
Hot Wheels Toy Car Track Set Hill Climb Champion with 1:64 Scale Car, Launch Uphill to Score Points & Win Amazon was temporarily out of stock so I grabbed this from another source. We are an avid Hot Wheels family and always like to check out the newer sets. I love the idea of running a car around a course continuously, without relying on batteries. This set comes with a big launcher, that features a unique track with protruding tabs that catch the cars from behind as you blast them around the track. The whole idea is to catch the car(s) at the right time when it reenters the launcher, so you can have it racing around the course non-stop. Unfortunately, the course is too small and uninteresting, yet, if the layout was much larger, that launcher wouldn't have enough force without some kind of midway helper (like an automatic loop launcher). This would make a world of a difference in fun, so you you're not pounding the launcher every half second to keep the car circulating around a tiny oval which gets old fast.

Big annoyance: The launcher is very tall, so it comes in packed in two pieces which easily lock together, however, once locked, you're unable to seperate them. This is now the second set we have with this annoying problem. We like storing our hot wheels in their boxes, but once opened, there's no way to get this giant launcher back inside. Even if storing out of the box, with other toys, it's a big jalopy that could have been dismantled, taking up less space.

And finally, kids need laser-sharp hand/eye coordination to catch the car on time, so this may frustrate the impatient type. When you do manage to catch the car to keep it going, it does feel rewarding, even if it's only 2 laps. We haven't tried more than one car at a time, but I imagine on a large course, it must be fun, but on this small circuit, it's probably near impossible to work with.
text_fidelity_b: Hot Wheels Toy Car Track Set Hill Climb Champion with 1:64 Scale Car, Launch Uphill to Score Points & Win

text_fidelity_a: Alex Jr. Tots First Chunky Pegs Baby Toddler Sorting Activity This was a surprise Christmas gift hit with both my toddlers.  My 18 month old really enjoys it. My children have never played with this one toy for long periods, but it is a nice part of some play time and has no annoying bells and whistles.  I wouldn't be surprised if this toy doesn't necessarily last long for either of my children, but I can also see them using the pegs for different things as they outgrow the obvious first use as well as the base as part of their kitchen or playdoh or growing plants etc.

text_fidelity_a:
Mountains Out of Molehills | Family Board Game for 2-4 Players | Two-Level Gameboard Featuring Unique Gameplay & Custom Artwork | Great Gateway Game for Ages 9+ This game hits that sweet spot where the complexity is enough for adults but not so high that kids struggle. And it’s FUN! It says 9 and up but my 7-year-old caught on pretty quickly and was delighted when we talked about it in terms of executing a program. My family loves this game. My husband and I can see playing it with just adults too.

The gameplay involves drafting cards and then using them to create a plan for how the mole will move on the grid, which is essentially a simple program much like one would write on a computer. It takes some strategy, but you can only predict other people so much and this is where the game shines.

I was worried it would be too complex or long when we read the rules, but it plays very smoothly! We felt comfortable within 2 rounds, and it was a lot of fun seeing how the plans we made would be thwarted as other players move. We also enjoyed how the turn order changed. There are many levels of subtle strategy, I feel like we will be learning new things each time we play. There is a random element of dice when placing a rock on the board, simple but genius game design. It keeps it from feeling unfair, and adds an element of luck to using it.

Even when you are losing, it’s so interesting to see the programs unfold as each card flips that it didn’t feel upsetting, and most of the points are earned in the later rounds as the mounds get higher so you can easily catch back up to an early lead or after a bad round. This means you don’t feel too discouraged if you have a poor start.

I like that it has a defined timeline, there are 6 rounds and you know what they will look like. Overall a great choice for a family game night as it is not likely to overrun an hour.

The double-layer boards and gameplay are unique and the story of the moles is full of flavor. The art is charming and the explanation of the rules such as “moles are too polite so they don’t move when they hit another” is a really sweet touch. The printing is great quality, the game is just beautiful to look at. The box is well-organized making setup and takedown easy, and it looks pretty on the shelf. Plus, we love the moles! The standees make great pieces. This game shows a lot of care in the details, and we love games with a lot of artistic flavor.

text_fidelity_a:
Easy Bake Ultimate Oven, Pink/Purple I got the Easy Bake Ultimate Oven for my little boy. What woman doesn't love it when a man can cook?! ;) He's almost 3, so not quite the targeted age, but we still had fun with it.

What we like:
-I like that it's purple, which is a LITTLE bit more on the neutral side.
-It cooks very quickly. You preheat for 20 minutes and then cook an average of 10 minutes or so. You get exact directions, though. I was expecting a MUCH longer cook time.

What we didn't like:
-You can't watch the food while it cooks. I wish the front was clear, and it would have made this a much better learning tool, and made it a lot more fun.
-The portions are TINY! Seriously, I don't think it would fill up a mouse! But, I guess I have to expect tiny portions for it to cook so quickly. And, I think it's more of a "time together" kind of activity!

Just some neutral information we learned. You can cook "regular" food in the oven. If you're like us, you can't pay a lot of money for tiny mixes that produce 1/10th of the size of a normal cookie. Just save a little batter from when you cook. I also learned that you CAN burn food in this oven. :) So make sure you set a timer.
The pictures in the directions have cute, perfect little cookies and cupcakes. Ours didn't even come close to looking that great. Maybe with a little more practice?!
This oven comes with a batch of cookies and cupcakes w/frosting, sugar crystals, and cupcake wraps. It also has two cooking pans and an "arm" to push the pans into the oven. It has spots marked to make sure you get them to the correct spot to cook and cool. Overall, we've had a lot of fun with it!

And this is probably obvious, but it's electric. ;)
text_fidelity_b: Easy Bake Ultimate Oven, Pink/Purple

Mountains Out of Molehills | Family Board Game for 2-4 Players | Two-Level Gameboard Featuring Unique Gameplay & Custom Artwork | Great Gateway Game for Ages 9+ This is a good programmable movement game for 2 - 4 players. You draft a set of movement cards, then organize them into a plan of action for your turn, and you let your mole loose on the dirt. Everywhere you pass, you add to the pile of dirt until your dirt piles get so large that they topple over, which usually happens near the end of every game...

...but the real fun of this game is the rock. If your mole hits the rock, which moves around each round at the whim of the player who drafts the right card, then you bump, switch directions, and watch your plan fail and falter. It's funny, even for the person who gets messed up because of it.

So this is a very fun game that is light and easy to learn. I wish the underground was a little clearer in terms of where the spaces are, or that the moles were a little bit better sized for the pieces. It works though.

text_fidelity_a:
Moose Racing Mission: Diamond Heist Game Board with Spy, Challenges and Instructions, Multi (91009) This is a really cool and interesting game! I wasn't sure what to expect based on the box and description, but unlike other contraption based games I've played (like the classic "mouse trap" from my youth), this is more of a cooperative play game.
There are 4 strings that move a (clearly mission-impossible inspired) suspended character around the playing board, and it takes careful pulling and releasing each of them as a group effort to navigate properly, sort of like a marionette puppet meets a corporate team building activity. There are some things to do like remove security cameras and traps but the truth is, the real fun doesn't start until you open up the jewel cage.
Once the cage is open, there's a countdown (you can hear the spring noise whirring as soon as it opens) and the police car starts to slowly circle the board. If you make it to the getaway car with the jewel before the car makes it to block your path, you win! If, however, you take too long, the police car will spring into place and block your path. Hilarity ensues as players start to panic and lose their cool, and in the end, whether you make it or not, it felt exciting.
Things I like about the game:
- It is cooperative, not individual. So you don't "beat" another player, you work as a team to complete the task in time.
- The mechanical game board is unique and really fun to learn
- It does NOT require batteries! The board uses spring loaded timers where necessary, no electricity. This is cool in a decidedly analog way.
- People can walk over and see how it is played and join with very little instruction

Things I did not, however, like:
- The truth is, when playing with my kids, we sort of skipped the first part of the game and just jumped to the jewel part. The designers of this game tried to make it longer by adding disarming traps and pulling security cameras in particular order based on cards, but it felt tedious after a few rounds. Really the fun part is the end. The whirring police car gives a sense of danger and urgency that makes it fun.
- That little spy is suspended by strings that get tangled so quickly and easily. It feels like I sneeze and they are tangled. Out of the box, I had to spend time untwisting it before we played for the first time, so be careful.

That being said, the game is TON of fun for different ages and we actually had some guests come over who looked at it and wanted to play too (adults AND kids). They all asked where to to get it, so it might become a regular thing found in our neighborhood. I'd say it deserves 5 stars, it's been a while since a game sparked this much interest that wasn't on a screen.
text_fidelity_b: Moose Racing Mission: Diamond Heist Game Board with Spy, Challenges and Instructions, Multi (91009)

Hasbro Gaming Sorry Spin My family has really enjoyed playing this updated version of an old favorite. The basic rules are the same as in the original Sorry! Each player has four pawns to move around the board from Start to Home. You draw a card to find out how many spaces you can move your game piece. Landing on another player's pawn sends them back to start as does the Sorry! card, just as in the classic version.

What's different about Sorry Spin is the spinning board. The center circle is the main board, with connecting circles for each color's home which fit together like gears. The challenge of the spinning board is your home is contantly changing position in relation to the main board. You may be just a few spaces away from reaching your home track when the board will spin and you will end up all the way across the board from your home.

It took about 5 minutes to assemble the game board, which seems very sturdy. We had some trouble spinning the board on a slick surface (wood table, counter top), but when we placed it on a placemat, it worked fine. A nice addition is a box that can be assembled and used to store the cards.

This is a great family game which is faster paced than the original version of the game due to the spinning board and a shorter path between start and home. Also any number gets a pawn out of start. (unlike the original which requires a 1 or 2). Older kids and adults will enjoy the suggested variation of the two-player game in which each person selects two different colors instead of only one.
text_fidelity_b: Hasbro Gaming Sorry Spin

text_fidelity_a:
Playskool Showcam 2-in-1 Digital Camera and Projector (Gray) For my daughter's sake, I would give this camera 5 stars. It is the longest lasting favorite toy any of my kids have ever received, EVER. I bought it for my then 7 year old daughter for Christmas 2 years ago, and it is still her very favorite toy at age 9. She plays with it almost daily, takes it with her on trips and to important events, and shows everyone the pictures she takes. I think not much more praise can be had for a toy than for it to be beloved after two full years of daily play! But I wills say, her expectations for it are different than mine. She doesn't care about printing the pictures out. She likes taking them and looking at them on the viewfinder, projecting them on the wall, and using the added features to make funny frames around the people and funny sounds. That's all she wants from it, and it delivers that perfectly.

BUT, as a parent, I would have hoped the screen would be better quality. When you look at it, it's sort of blurry and got lines through it. Frankly, sometimes it's hard to tell what I'm looking at. This doesn't bother my now 9 year old daughter AT ALL. But it is disappointing to me because I know the technology exists to make that better.

The quality of pictures is also not great when uploaded onto my computer (which I've only done a couple of times). It's VERY pixelated. Again, this isn't a feature my daughter cares about, so take that into account, but for me I wish that the option were there to print out a decent quality print because sometimes she takes really awesome shots that I wish I could save.

This camera is also super tough. Despite being dropped and thrown around and fought over by siblings for the last 2 years, it still works perfectly. The batteries last her generally a few months, depending on play. But they're just AA's, so no biggie to change them out.

Really, I am most impressed that this toy continues to make her so happy. I think Playskool could go a long way to making the picture/screen quality better, even for kids, but that's just a mom talking!
text_fidelity_b: Playskool Showcam 2-in-1 Digital Camera and Projector (Gray)

text_fidelity_a:
The Adventures of Robin Hood | A Kosmos Game | Family-Friendly, Cooperative, Role-Player, Story-Driven Game for 2 to 4 Players, Ages 10 and up Several years ago there was a British series about Robin Hood, and my family and I have been hooked ever since seeing that series. This game seemed like a good fit for my family based on our interests, and so far it has been a good addition to family game night. That said, this game tends to be on the easy side and the replayability isn't great if you want a varying experience.

In a nutshell, this is a basic move-around-the-board game at its heart, though it requires cooperation instead of competition and it relies on a story book to further the game along. Some real time and attention to detail went into the design and it shows.

Though the game does not require following a path without turning to the left or right, it does follow a basic flow and the story book is designed to help guide and direct. That said, it essentially is a map of how to get through each step and it does not vary from game to game so once the game has been played the book could potentially slow down a game instead of moving it along at an interesting pace since previous players will know what to do.

This is certainly not a bad game. It's a good family game and is worth running through as a group. However, for those looking for replayability, this one lacks variety.
text_fidelity_b: The Adventures of Robin Hood | A Kosmos Game | Family-Friendly, Cooperative, Role-Player, Story-Driven Game for 2 to 4 Players, Ages 10 and up
